Installation of roof-mounted, grid-tied 30.2kW solar PV system including 116, 260 watt Solar World modules and a solar edge inverter system.

Altenergy will be installing a 14.57 kW solar PV system on the roof of the Madison Investments 5th Street development, comprised of 47 Axitec 310W polycrystalline PV modules. Modules are installed on the roof using the Ecolibrium EcoFoot 2+ ballasted racking system. Modules are wired directly to a DC optimizer mounted under each panel. Modules/optimizers are wired in series with 16 optimizers wired in two strings and 15 in the third string. The DC power from the optimizer strings will be combined on the roof and wired externally on the building in metallic conduit down to the inverter located inside next to the main electrical panel in the electrical room. The AC power from the inverter will be run to an AC disconnect outside next to the meter and then back into the main service panel to make a supply-side connection with Ilsco insulated piercing taps.

GRID Alternatives Mid-Atlantic, on behalf of the District of Columbias Department of General Services (DGS) and Department of Energy and Environment, plans to install a 2.65MW DC ground-mounted CREF composed of 7,280 photovoltaic solar modules and 12 string inverters. A variety of construction activities will be required prior to installing photovoltaic solar modules and string inverters. Initial tasks will include clearing the 4.5-acre system footprint of existing refuse and overgrowth, renovation of existing site entrance gate, installation of a new 8ft perimeter fence including lockable gate entrance, driving of 846 I-Beam pilings, and erection of 286 solar racks. Following the installation of photovoltaic solar modules, electrical services will tie the ground-mounted solar system to the PEPCO utility grid via new electrical line extension. Additional electrical tasks will include installation of transformers and other medium-voltage electrical gear on a concrete pad and mounted to 55ft utility poles.
Stormwater Management and Soil and Erosion Control methods will be enacted to limit the potential of negative environmental and community impacts resulting from the construction process. These methods will include installation of a stabilized construction entrance with wash rack and use of straw bale dykes along the sites Northwest and Southwest perimeter. Post construction activities will be limited to sporadic system troubleshooting and systematic mowing of overgrowth to take place on an as-needed basis. Landscaping services will follow completion of the construction process and will be driven by the District of Columbias Department of Energy and Environment.

The solar array will consist of 2,444 solar modules, each with 470 Watts of power, for a total of 1148.68 kilowatts of clean energy capacity. The total square footage of the proposed array would be 70,980 square feet, remaining fully within the existing parking structure footprint. A total of fifty-two (52) piers would be attached to the existing building structure to support the array. 

The solar canopy will be a Community Solar Energy Facility (CREF), developed in conjunction with the District of Columbias Department of Energy and Environments Solar for All program. The energy generated by the CREF will be donated to low- and moderate-income residents in Washington, DC. The energy generated by the array would help the District of Columbia meet its ambitious sustainability goals and renewable portfolio standard (RPS).

(26.64 kW DC) on the roof of Borough residence.
The PV modules will be mounted on the roof with the Everest D Dome R2 ballasted racking
system. Modules will be wired with each individual modules output circuit run to the AP
systems micro-inverters mounted underneath the PV modules on the roof. The output of
each inverter will be connected to the AP systems QS1 AC Bus Cable with three inverters
connected to each cable running to its own dedicated 20 A breaker.
The inverters outputs will be combined in an "AC combiner" panel where each inverter output
circuit will be combined into a single output circuit. From the AC combiner panel, the
combined output will run to a dedicated solar AC disconnect. From the disconnect, a load
side connection will be made into the main electric service panel with a back-fed breaker.
